layers.title: Castle rock
layers.intro: The sandstone rock at the western end of the old town has been the site of Nottingham's castle since 1068. Kings held court here, the Civil War began below it, and the mansion that replaced the castle was burned in 1831 and later became the city's museum. Old inns and caves lie at its foot.

layers.title: Market Square
layers.intro: The Old Market Square was the centre of Nottingham for centuries. It lay where the town's Saxon and Norman settlements met, and was for long the site of the town's markets, fairs and government. The surrounding streets hold some of the city's oldest inns and many of its theatres and halls.

groups.title: The market
groups.intro: The great Market Place was where the town traded, held Goose Fair and gathered for public events, from the cheese riot of 1766 to parliamentary elections. The Exchange, built in the 1720s, housed the Corporation, and its replacement, the Council House of 1929, still dominates the square.

groups.title: Houses, hotels and halls
groups.intro: As the town grew richer in the 18th and 19th centuries, the streets around the square filled with substantial buildings: a Georgian town house that became a subscription library, theatres, a hotel and music halls. Several have been put to new uses, as Rock City shows.

groups.title: Shops
groups.intro: Around 1900 the streets off the square filled with new shops built to catch the eye. Two of them, for a grocer and for Boots, carry some of the city's rare Art Nouveau decoration.

layers.title: Lace Market
layers.intro: The hill east of the Market Square was the site of the Saxon town, taken by the Danes in 868 and centred on St Mary's Church. In the 19th century lace merchants built their warehouses and showrooms here, giving the district its name. Below it lay the marshy ground of Broad Marsh.

groups.title: Lace Market
items: The body snatchers of Barker Gate, 1827

layers.title: North of the centre
layers.intro: North of the old town lay open fields and common land until the 19th century. As Nottingham expanded, the area was used for public parks and cemeteries, a Catholic cathedral, a college and a great railway station. It is now part of the city centre.

layers.title: Sneinton
layers.intro: Sneinton lies on the hill east of the city. Its windmill belonged to the family of the mathematician George Green, William Booth was born here in 1829, and the city's wholesale market moved here in the 1930s. Cave dwellings were once dug into its sandstone ridge.

layers.title: St Ann's
layers.intro: St Ann's takes its name from a medieval well once thought to heal. Its hillside allotments are among the oldest in England, and after enclosure in 1845 the fields were covered with dense terraced housing, much of which was cleared and rebuilt around 1970.

layers.title: The Meadows
layers.intro: The Meadows, the low ground between the city and the Trent, was built over with terraced housing before the First World War. The area was protected by the Victoria Embankment, is home to Notts County's ground, and was largely rebuilt in the 1970s.

layers.title: Hockley
layers.intro: Hockley lies below the Lace Market, where Nottingham's cloth workers gave the medieval street Walker Gate its name. In the 18th century Arkwright built his first cotton mill here, Methodists opened a chapel, and in 1849 John Boot opened his shop on Goose Gate. More recently it has become known for its independent cinemas.

groups.title: Hockley
items: Pulp Fiction and the Screen Room

layers.title: The Park Estate
layers.intro: The Park began as the castle's deer park. From the 1820s the Dukes of Newcastle developed it as a private estate of villas for the well-to-do, many designed by T. C. Hine, and its streets are still lit by gas.

groups.title: The Park Estate
items: Sold, saved and run by its residents

layers.title: Castle Marina
layers.intro: The Nottingham Canal, opened in 1796, brought coal and goods into the town, and wharves and warehouses grew up along it west of the centre. When the canal trade declined, the old railway sidings beside it were dug out in the 1980s for a marina.

layers.title: Wilford
layers.intro: Wilford is a village on the south bank of the Trent, linked to Nottingham for centuries by ferry and, from 1870, by a toll bridge. Its church, manor and inn record a long rural history; in the late 19th century it became a suburb.

groups.title: Ford, manor and church
groups.intro: Wilford's history begins at the river: remains of a Roman ford were found here in 1900. The manor is recorded in Domesday Book, and the church of St Wilfrid was founded in the 14th century.

groups.title: The village and its big house
groups.intro: From the 17th to the early 19th century Wilford was a quiet riverside village, centred on its inn and, from 1781, on Wilford House. Among its residents were a sea captain, a poet and the leader of the Pentrich rising.

groups.title: Bridges, coal and the suburb
groups.intro: From the late 1860s Wilford changed rapidly. A colliery was opened, a toll bridge replaced the ferry in 1870, and the population almost doubled in the 1890s. In 1925 a power station was built on the opposite bank.

groups.title: Sportsmen of Wilford
groups.intro: Wilford produced several notable footballers in the late 19th and early 20th centuries, among them Harry Cursham of Notts County and two Iremongers.

groups.title: War and the trams
groups.intro: The churchyard holds the graves of servicemen from both World Wars. In 2015 the tram reached Wilford, linking the village to the city again.

layers.title: West Bridgford
layers.intro: West Bridgford, across the Trent from the city, grew from a small village into a large suburb from the late 19th century. It is the home of Trent Bridge cricket ground, of Nottingham Forest's City Ground, and of the county council.

groups.title: Trent Bridge
groups.intro: The southern end of Trent Bridge has been defended and settled since the 10th century. In the 19th century the land beside it became a cricket ground, which hosted its first Test in 1899, and in 1898 Nottingham Forest moved to the City Ground nearby.

groups.title: Bridgford & Lady Bay
groups.intro: The old village of West Bridgford grew up around St Giles' Church. The Musters family held the estate from 1523, and when they sold land for building the suburb spread, reaching Lady Bay by the river, where bombs fell in 1941 and floods in 1947.

groups.title: Edwalton
groups.intro: Edwalton was a small village with a medieval church, given a station on the new railway in 1880. The district of Compton Acres was built beside it in the 1990s.

layers.title: Clifton
layers.intro: For centuries Clifton was the village of the Clifton family, who held the manor from the 13th century. After the Second World War the council built a very large housing estate beside it, changing the area completely, while the old village survived on its hill above the Trent.

groups.title: Before the village
items: A Roman farm by the A453
groups.intro: Long before the village grew up, a farm stood on the higher ground to its south-west, from around the time of the Roman conquest.

groups.title: The village
items: The thatched houses of Village Road
groups.intro: The old village grew up around the Cliftons' hall and the parish church, which dates from about 1190. Its almshouses, dovecote and school were provided by the family and other benefactors, and some of its houses go back to the medieval period.

groups.title: Clifton Grove
groups.intro: Below the village the land runs down to the Trent. Bronze Age remains have been found here, the Cliftons planted an avenue of elms in 1677, and the grove became the setting of a popular ballad. In 1958 Clifton Bridge was built nearby to relieve Trent Bridge.

groups.title: The estate and its people
groups.intro: In 1801 the village had fewer than 400 people. From the 1950s the council built a large estate beside it. The footballer Viv Anderson was born in Clifton in 1956.

layers.title: Barton in Fabis
layers.intro: Barton in Fabis is a small farming village on the south bank of the Trent. Its name records the beans once grown in its fields, and its medieval church and 17th-century dovecote reflect a long agricultural history, with a ferry linking it across the river.

layers.title: Thrumpton
layers.intro: Thrumpton is a small estate village on the Trent. Its hall was built by the Pigot family in the early 17th century, and later owners built much of the village. The estate has passed through several families, including the Byrons.

layers.title: Ruddington
layers.intro: Ruddington was a village of framework knitters south of the city, and its workshops are now a museum. Nearby stood the medieval church of Flawford, demolished in 1779, and in the 20th century a railway station and an ammunition depot were built on the village's edge.

layers.title: Gotham
layers.intro: Gotham is best known for the tales of its 'Wise Men', the fools of Gotham, already told in the 15th century. Its name later gave New York the nickname 'Gotham'. The village also had its medieval church and, from the late 19th century, gypsum mining.

layers.title: Ratcliffe-on-Soar
layers.intro: Ratcliffe-on-Soar is a small village by the River Soar, near the southern edge of the county. It was overshadowed from 1968 by its coal-fired power station, which in 2024 became the last in Britain to close. A main-line station was built nearby in 2008.

layers.title: Holme Pierrepont
layers.intro: Holme Pierrepont, on the flat land along the Trent east of the city, was held by the Pierrepont family from the 13th century. Their Tudor brick hall and family church still stand. In the 20th century plans for a large power station here were dropped, and the gravel workings became the National Watersports Centre.

groups.title: Holme Pierrepont
items: The power station that was not built

layers.title: Shelford
layers.intro: Shelford, on the Trent, was the site of an Augustinian priory. After the Dissolution the Stanhope family acquired the land, and their house was garrisoned for the King in the Civil War until Parliament's forces stormed it in 1645.

layers.title: Tollerton
layers.intro: Tollerton is a village south-east of the city with a 12th-century church. Its hall became a Catholic seminary in 1948, and the airfield nearby, opened in 1930, was one of the first municipal aerodromes in Britain.

layers.title: Cotgrave
layers.intro: Cotgrave has a long history, from an Anglo-Saxon burial ground and a 12th-century church to its transformation in the 1960s, when a new colliery brought mining families from closed pits and the village grew several times over.

layers.title: Radford
layers.intro: Radford was a village west of Nottingham whose church belonged to Lenton Priory. In the 19th century it became one of the city's main industrial districts, home to Raleigh's bicycle works and Player's tobacco factories, and the setting of Alan Sillitoe's Saturday Night and Sunday Morning.

layers.title: Lenton
layers.intro: Lenton was dominated for over four centuries by its Cluniac priory, founded in about 1102 and dissolved in 1538. Industrial growth came in the 19th century, with Raleigh's bicycle works, and in the 20th the University of Nottingham was built at Highfields, where MRI was later developed.

groups.title: Lenton
items: A brain scanner you can wear, 2018

layers.title: Wollaton
layers.intro: Wollaton was the village of the Willoughby family, who also worked coal here. Their Elizabethan hall, built in the 1580s, still dominates the park, and as early as 1603–04 a wooden wagonway carried coal from their pits. The last colliery here closed in 1965.

layers.title: Beeston
layers.intro: Beeston grew from a village into an industrial town in the 19th and 20th centuries. Its silk mill was burned in the Reform riots of 1831, Thomas Humber built his bicycle works here around 1878, and in the 1930s Boots built its large factories on the town's edge.

layers.title: Chilwell
layers.intro: Chilwell began as a hamlet on the road to Ashby-de-la-Zouch, where Roman finds show earlier settlement. It grew into a suburb in the 20th century, and in the First World War it was the site of the National Shell Filling Factory, where an explosion killed 134 people in 1918.

layers.title: Giltbrook
layers.intro: Giltbrook, named after the stream that runs through it, lies in the Erewash valley. In 1817 the Pentrich rebels, marching on Nottingham, were dispersed nearby, and in the 1870s the Great Northern Railway built its long viaduct, the Forty Bridges, across the valley.

layers.title: Eastwood
layers.intro: Eastwood was a mining town on the Nottinghamshire–Derbyshire border. In 1832 local coal owners met at the Sun Inn to plan a railway, which became part of the Midland Railway, and in 1885 D. H. Lawrence was born here, the son of a miner.

groups.title: Eastwood
items: The railway that began in a pub

layers.title: Bennerley
layers.intro: In the Erewash valley, on the border of Nottinghamshire and Derbyshire, coal and iron were worked side by side in the 19th century. The ironworks at Bennerley and the wrought-iron viaduct built in 1876–77 belong to that industrial landscape, much of it undermined by coal workings.

layers.title: Attenborough
layers.intro: Attenborough is an old village on the Trent, known in Saxon times as Addensburgh. The Civil War general Henry Ireton came from here, and its churchyard holds the memorial to those killed in the Chilwell explosion of 1918. Gravel digging in the 20th century left the lakes of the nature reserve.

layers.title: Stapleford
layers.intro: Stapleford is an old village west of the city with an Anglo-Saxon cross of about AD 1000 in its churchyard. On the hill nearby stands the Hemlock Stone, a natural sandstone pillar surrounded by legend.

layers.title: Arnold
layers.intro: Arnold was a Domesday village north of Nottingham that grew into a town of hosiery and cotton. Its mill owners and framework knitters were part of the county's textile industry, and in 1811 the Luddite frame-breaking began here. The painter Richard Parkes Bonington and the water engineer Thomas Hawksley were both born in Arnold.

layers.title: Calverton
layers.intro: Calverton has two claims to a place in history. William Lee, who invented the stocking frame in 1589, came from here, and in 1952 a new colliery opened that quadrupled the village's population within a decade.

layers.title: Gedling
layers.intro: Gedling was a farming village east of the city, with a 13th-century church. From 1899 its colliery was the main local employer for almost a century; the railway station that served it closed in 1960, and the colliery site has since become a country park.

layers.title: Bestwood
layers.intro: Bestwood began as a royal hunting park, recorded from 1286. In the 19th century it belonged to the Dukes of St Albans, who built a new lodge, and in the 1870s and 1880s its colliery and ironworks brought industry and a new village to the old parkland.

layers.title: Papplewick
layers.intro: Papplewick lies on the River Leen north of Nottingham. In the late 18th century cotton mills were built along the river and Papplewick Hall was built nearby, and in the 1880s a pumping station was built here to raise drinking water for the growing city.

layers.title: Hucknall
layers.intro: Hucknall was a village of framework knitters that became a mining town after its collieries opened in the 1860s. Lord Byron is buried in its parish church. From 1927 Rolls-Royce tested aero engines at its airfield, and in 2004 the tram arrived.

layers.title: Basford
layers.intro: Basford, recorded in Domesday Book, lay along the River Leen. In the 19th century the river's clean water drew bleachers, and the village became an industrial suburb with breweries, a sauce factory and a soap works. It was also home to the poet Philip James Bailey and the motorcycle maker George Brough.

layers.title: Bulwell
layers.intro: Bulwell, recorded in Domesday Book, was a market town on the River Leen with its own trades: limestone quarrying, glove-making and bleaching. Its people defended their common land, the Bogs, when the lord of the manor tried to enclose it in 1872.

layers.title: Sherwood
layers.intro: Sherwood grew up along Mansfield Road, the old main road north from Nottingham. A Georgian house is its oldest building, and in the 19th century the area was laid out for housing, reached by tram from 1900.

layers.title: Mapperley
layers.intro: Mapperley takes its name from Thomas Mapurley, a 14th-century official. The high ground north-east of the town was the estate of the Wright family, and in the 19th century it was chosen for hospitals and asylums. Its clay also supplied some of the area's largest brickworks.

layers.title: Carlton
layers.intro: Carlton was a small township of farmers and framework knitters east of Nottingham. In the 19th century the textile trade and the railway made it a growing suburb, with a new church built by the Earl of Carnarvon and brickworks on the hill.

layers.title: People
layers.intro: People connected with buildings on the map: who designed them, who lived, worked or played in them, and who is remembered on their walls. Entries come from commemorative plaques (Open Plaques), architects recorded in Wikidata, and hand-written entries checked against Wikipedia and Historic England.

layers.title: Long Eaton
layers.intro: Long Eaton, recorded in Domesday Book, remained a village until the railway arrived in 1839. It then grew rapidly, with a large railway yard nearby and, from the 1850s, lace mills, and its new prosperity can be seen in its Edwardian and Art Nouveau buildings.

groups.title: Long Eaton
items: The Great Fire of Long Eaton

layers.title: Ilkeston
layers.intro: Ilkeston, on a hill above the Erewash, received a market charter from Henry III in 1252 and still holds its charter fair. The town grew with the coal and iron industries of the Erewash valley, especially the Stanton ironworks. It lost its railway stations in the 20th century and regained one in 2017.

layers.title: Broxtowe
layers.intro: Broxtowe is a council estate in the north-west of the city, in Aspley ward, perhaps named after Broxtowe Hall, which was pulled down in 1937. Building the estate brought much older finds to light.

layers.title: Kimberley and Watnall
layers.intro: Kimberley, north-west of the city, grew as a centre of coal mining, brewing and hosiery. In the Second World War neighbouring Watnall held the headquarters of the RAF's fighter group for the Midlands.

layers.title: Linby
layers.intro: Linby is a village north of Hucknall, with an old stone cross at each end, and the remains of Annesley Hall's south lodge gates nearby.

layers.title: Bingham
layers.intro: Bingham is a market town east of Nottingham. A field at its eastern end holds earthworks long taken for a lost medieval village.

layers.title: Plumtree
layers.intro: Plumtree is a small village south-east of Nottingham. Its church of St Mary is believed to be one of the oldest in the county.

layers.title: Names and beginnings
layers.intro: Before anything here was written down, people left their names on the land and their things in the ground.

gata.title: Nottingham (East Midlands Vikings, University of Nottingham)

groups.title: Before the English, c. 1000 BC–AD 400
groups.intro: The Roman road called the Fosse Way was built in the first and second centuries AD, from Exeter in the south-west to Lincoln in the north-east, and crossed this county with a stopping place at Castle Hill near Bingham.[^fosse]

groups.title: The English settle, 6th–10th centuries
groups.intro: Most places in England still bear Old English names, and many of them hold the names of the settlers who founded them.[^oe] Nottingham is one: Snotingaham, the homestead of the Snotingas, the people of a man called Snot.[^snot]

groups.title: The Danes, 868–924
groups.intro: From 877 Danish armies settled the East Midlands, each round a fortified town: Derby, Leicester, Lincoln, Nottingham and Stamford, the Five Boroughs.[^five] They left names of their own, such as -by for a village and -thorpe for an outlying farm,[^norse] and in Nottingham the streets called -gate, from the Old Norse gata, a road: Barker Gate, Castle Gate, Fisher Gate.[^gata]

groups.title: Domesday Book, 1086
groups.intro: In 1085 the king sent his agents to survey every shire in England, to record what was owed to him and who now held the land. Its name came from the Last Judgement: from its record, as from that, there was no appeal.[^dom]

groups.title: Names given since, 1285–1807
groups.intro: After the Norman Conquest some places gained a second part to their name, the name of the family that now held them,[^manor] but England's place-names have changed little since the early Norman period.[^stable] The new names went to streets, districts and springs.

layers.title: Roman times
layers.intro: Before the Romans this was the land of the Corieltauvi, a Celtic tribe of the East Midlands whose capital was at Leicester, and there is little sign that they fought the conquest.[^cor] No Roman town stood where Nottingham is now: the traces of those centuries lie around it.

groups.title: The army, 1st century AD
groups.intro: For the first few decades after the invasion of AD 43, the Fosse Way, which crossed this county, marked the western frontier of Roman rule.[^fosse]

groups.title: Farms and villas, 1st–4th centuries
items: A Roman farm by the A453
groups.intro: The Romans brought better farming, and by the 4th century lowland Britain was prosperous enough to send grain across the sea. That wealth paid for a blossoming of villa building and decoration between AD 300 and 350.[^rb]

groups.title: By the rivers, Roman times
groups.intro: Roman builders paved fords with flagstones on timber piles, as at Littleborough further down the Trent, where a Roman road crossed the river to the town of Segelocum.[^trent]

layers.title: Castle and Crown
layers.intro: After the Norman Conquest William the Conqueror built a castle at Nottingham and gave it into the keeping of William Peverel.[^nott] For six centuries it was the Crown's; then it was the dukes'; at last it was the town's.

groups.title: The royal castle, 1068–1600
groups.intro: William also made Sherwood a royal hunting forest, under forest laws, covering perhaps a quarter of the county; King John and Edward I hunted there.[^sher] The castle was the kings' house beside it.

groups.title: The Civil War, 1642–1651
groups.intro: The war grew out of a long struggle between the monarchy and Parliament for political and religious control. When the fighting began in August 1642, Charles left York for Nottingham, close to the Royalist Midlands.[^ecw]

groups.title: The dukes' mansion, 1663–1831
groups.intro: William Cavendish had fought for the King and gone into exile. At the Restoration he came home and won back most of his estates, and in 1665 he was made Duke of Newcastle.[^cav]

groups.title: The castle museum, 1878
groups.intro: From 1845 Parliament let boroughs of 10,000 people or more raise a halfpenny rate to set up museums.[^mus]

layers.title: The Civil War
layers.intro: The war grew out of a long struggle between the monarchy and Parliament for political and religious control.[^ecw] Nottingham was where it began, and a Parliament town through all of it, with Royalist garrisons round it.

groups.title: The King's standard, 1642
groups.intro: That year Parliament claimed command of the county militias, and Charles answered with commissions of his own. When the fighting began in August, both sides believed one battle would settle it.[^militia]

groups.title: Holding the castle, 1643–1645
groups.intro: The enemy was close. Newark, where the Great North Road met the Fosse Way and crossed the Trent, was a Royalist stronghold, besieged three times; it held out until the King ordered it to surrender in May 1646.[^newark]

groups.title: Shelford and the end of the castle, 1645–1651
groups.intro: When the war ended, Parliament made many castles useless, slighting them so that they could not be held against it again.[^slight]

layers.title: Frames and lace
layers.intro: For three centuries Nottingham lived by its textiles. The hosiery trade settled in the town after 1730, and with its offshoot, lace, it came to dominate the town's economy through the 18th and 19th centuries.[^hist]

groups.title: Wool and the frame, 1285–1728
groups.intro: Wool was one of the most important parts of medieval England's economy, and English wool was prized across Europe.[^wool]

groups.title: Cotton mills, 1768–1791
groups.intro: In 1769 Richard Arkwright patented a spinning frame that twisted cotton into a strong yarn, fit for the warp threads that had been spun by hand, and it greatly reduced the cost of spinning.[^ark]

groups.title: Hard times, 1811–1831
groups.intro: The years 1810 to 1812 brought high unemployment and inflation, made worse by the cost of the wars with Napoleon, to a trade in which work was already notoriously precarious.[^hard]

groups.title: The Victorian trade, 1840–1865
groups.intro: The town grew so fast and so badly in these years that it came to have the worst slums in England.[^slums]

groups.title: Lace, 1813–1907
groups.intro: In 1808 John Heathcoat built a machine that made an exact imitation of pillow lace, a net called bobbinet, and patented it in 1809. In 1816 men believed to be paid by Nottingham lacemakers broke into his factory at Loughborough and destroyed 55 of its lace frames.[^heath]

groups.title: Lace remembered, 1969–2009
groups.intro: Lace declined as technology changed: by the 1970s fewer than 5,000 people worked in the Lace Market, and many of its factories stood derelict. In 1969 it became the city's first conservation area, and its warehouses have since found new uses.[^lm]

layers.title: Risings and riots
layers.intro: For a century and more, Nottingham's people took to the streets again and again. The town lived by hosiery, settled there after 1730, and later by lace,[^hist] trades in which work was notoriously precarious.[^dom] Few of those workers had a vote: before 1832 only about one Briton in twenty did.[^vote] And the town grew so fast and so badly that it came to have the worst slums in England.[^hist] Each chapter here is one outbreak, set against what lay behind it.

fields.title: Expansion (University of Nottingham Manuscripts and Special Collections)

groups.title: The cheese riot, 1766
groups.intro: Food riots were a familiar part of 18th-century life, with at least twelve major outbreaks. In 1766 poor harvests had already pushed up the price of grain, and when the first large-scale exports of it began that August, riots broke out across England; eight people were shot dead putting them down.[^food] Nottingham's came at its October fair.

groups.title: The Luddites, 1811
groups.intro: Stocking-knitters had taken organised action at times since 1675. The years 1810 to 1812 were hard ones, with high unemployment and inflation, made worse by the cost of the wars with Napoleon. The frame-breakers took their name from Ned Ludd, a probably mythical apprentice said to have smashed two stocking frames in 1779, and wrote as Captain, General or King Ludd.[^ludd]

groups.title: The Pentrich rising, 1817
groups.intro: Peace with France in 1815 brought no relief. Industrial change, demobilised soldiers and Corn Laws that kept bread dear drove the country into a deep depression. Radicals at Pentrich had their own Hampden Club, and the Home Office watched them through local magistrates and paid informers. The Pentrich men hoped to join a march on London in support of Sir Francis Burdett's bill for parliamentary reform.[^pent]

groups.title: The Reform riots, 1831
groups.intro: Parliament's seats had not been redrawn for population in many decades: some boroughs had a handful of voters, while Manchester had no MP at all. A bill to reform it passed the Commons in 1831, and its defeat in the Lords set off full-scale riots in Bristol and Derby as well as Nottingham.[^reform]

groups.title: The Chartists, 1842–1847
groups.intro: The People's Charter of 1838 asked for six reforms, among them a vote for every man over 21, the secret ballot and pay for MPs. The Commons refused to hear its first petition, of 1.3 million signatures, in 1839, and rejected the second, of over three million, in May 1842.[^charter] That summer, after employers had cut wages by up to a quarter in the slump, a general strike spread from Stalybridge and Ashton to Manchester and beyond.[^strike]

groups.title: The Bogs, 1872
groups.intro: Enclosure turned land held in common into private property.[^encl] Nottingham's burgesses, who held common rights in the town's fields, had held off their enclosure from 1787 until 1845, though it kept the town from growing outwards.[^fields] Who made the attempt on Bulwell's Bogs is unclear: Samuel Thomas Cooper, lord of the manor since he bought Bulwell Hall, had died the year before, in 1871.[^cooper]

groups.title: The St Ann's riots, 1958
groups.intro: St Ann's had been built after 1845 on the town's old Clay Fields, for the working poor, in terraces around courts; most of its houses had no inside toilet.[^stann] After the war people came from the Caribbean to work, in growing numbers from 1955, and met racism; by 1958 about one in ten of St Ann's people was not white.[^riot]

layers.title: Reform and the vote
layers.intro: The vote was won in steps: by the better-off in 1832,[^1832] by part of the urban working class in 1867,[^1867] by many country workers in 1884,[^1885] by women over 30 in 1918, and by all women, on the same terms as men, in 1928.[^equal]

equal.title: Women's suffrage in the United Kingdom

suff.title: Women's suffrage in the United Kingdom

groups.title: Reform, 1831–1832
groups.intro: The Act that passed in 1832 did away with the 56 smallest boroughs, gave two MPs each to 22 large towns, and gave the vote in the boroughs to men who paid a yearly rent of £10. The voters of England and Wales rose from about 400,000 to 650,000.[^1832a]

groups.title: The Chartists' MP, 1842–1847
groups.intro: The property qualifications of 1832 still kept most working men from the vote,[^1832b] and the Chartists wanted it for every man. Nottingham gave them the only MP they ever won.[^chartism]

groups.title: A vote for working men, 1865–1867
groups.intro: Before 1867 about one in seven of the adult men of England and Wales could vote. That year's Act gave the vote to part of the urban working class for the first time, and soon doubled their number.[^1867a]

groups.title: Three seats, 1884–1885
groups.intro: The Act of 1884 carried the household vote into the counties, to men such as miners and farm labourers. The next year's Redistribution of Seats Act put most MPs in seats of one member, and divided large towns so that their suburbs were represented apart from their centres.[^1885a]

groups.title: Votes for women, 1895–1918
groups.intro: In 1897 Millicent Fawcett founded the National Union of Women's Suffrage Societies, which pressed MPs by peaceful means. The Women's Social and Political Union, founded by the Pankhursts in 1903, turned militant; its members were the suffragettes.[^suff]

layers.title: Coal
layers.intro: Britain's coal output peaked in 1913, at 287 million tonnes;[^peak] its last deep mines closed in 2015.[^end] Nottinghamshire's pits, and the wagonways, canals, railways and power stations that served them, lie between those dates.

peak.title: Coal mining in the United Kingdom

end.title: Coal mining in the United Kingdom

men.title: Coal mining in the United Kingdom

ncb.title: Coal mining in the United Kingdom

groups.title: Wagons and canals, 1603–1839
items: The railway that began in a pub
groups.intro: The great age of canal building in England ran from the 1790s to the 1810s. The first canals were paid for by merchants, makers and mine owners who needed to ship their goods.[^canal]

groups.title: Deep pits and ironworks, 1861–1899
groups.intro: Coal employed more people in Britain than ever before or since in 1920, when 1,191,000 worked in it.[^men]

groups.title: Coal for power, 1925–2024
items: The power station that was not built
groups.intro: From 1926 a Central Electricity Board built Britain's first national grid, finished in September 1933. Later the biggest power stations were built on the coalfields themselves, such as West Burton, in the Nottinghamshire coalfield near the Trent.[^grid]

groups.title: The last pits, 1947–1999
groups.intro: On 1 January 1947 most mines passed to the new National Coal Board, and in the 1950s and 1960s closing pits became routine.[^ncb] After the strike of 1984–85 the Nottinghamshire miners split from the National Union of Mineworkers and formed a union of their own, the Union of Democratic Mineworkers, in December 1985.[^udm]

layers.title: Railways and roads
layers.intro: The canal, the railways, the trams and the airfields each came and grew, and most of them went; some have come back.

groups.title: Canal and carriage, 1796–1919
groups.intro: The great age of canal building in England ran from the 1790s to the 1810s, much of it paid for by mine owners and merchants who had goods to ship.[^canal]

groups.title: The railway comes, 1832–1880
items: The railway that began in a pub
groups.intro: In the railway mania of the 1840s, 263 Acts of Parliament were passed to set up new railway companies in 1846 alone, and about a third of the lines they allowed were never built.[^mania]

groups.title: The last main line, 1899–1904
groups.intro: The Great Central's line to London, opened in 1899, was the last main line built in Britain until High Speed 1 in 2003. Most of it closed between 1966 and 1969.[^gc]

groups.title: Trams, buses and trolleybuses, 1900–1966
groups.intro: A company had run horse and steam trams in Nottingham from 1877; the Corporation's electric trams began on 1 January 1901.[^tram]

groups.title: Into the air, 1916–1930
groups.intro: King George V founded the Royal Flying Corps on 13 April 1912. By the end of March 1918 it had some 150 squadrons, and on 1 April it was joined with the navy's air service as the Royal Air Force.[^rfc]

groups.title: Closures, 1947–1972
groups.intro: In 1963 the Beeching report picked out 2,363 stations and 5,000 miles of line for closure, and most of them closed as planned.[^beeching]

groups.title: Coming back, 1980s–2017
groups.intro: Britain's first modern street-running tramway opened in Manchester in 1992; until then Blackpool's, of 1885, was the only one of the first trams still running.[^metro] A few of the railways and stations closed in the 1960s have reopened too.[^reopen]

layers.title: Made in Nottingham
layers.intro: Nottingham became a city in 1897, as part of Queen Victoria's Diamond Jubilee.[^city] By then it made far more than lace, and three of its firms, Boots, Raleigh and Player's, became household names; by the end of the 20th century Raleigh and Player's had moved the bulk of their making elsewhere, while Boots thrived.[^three]

groups.title: Stone, clay and iron, 16th century–1860s
groups.intro: Before the town's famous firms, its ground was its first industry: what lay under it was dug, fired and smelted close to where it was found.

groups.title: Boots, 1849–1961
groups.intro: Boots is now one of the largest retailers in the UK and Ireland, by its sales and by its number of shops.[^boots]

groups.title: Beer, sauce and soap, 1852–1895
groups.intro: As the town grew, its pubs, kitchens and wash-houses were supplied from works on its edge.

groups.title: Clothes, 1865–1995
groups.intro: Clothes-making grew out of the stocking frame, and outlasted it.

groups.title: Wheels and engines, 1868–1960
groups.intro: By 1913 Raleigh was the largest bicycle manufacturing company in the world.[^raleigh]

groups.title: Tobacco, 1877–2016
groups.intro: John Player bought a tobacco business in 1877. In 1901 it merged with twelve other firms into the Imperial Tobacco Company, and by the late 1950s Player's employed 11,000 people.[^player]

layers.title: Markets and fairs
layers.intro: After the Normans, Nottingham was two boroughs, the English one round the old settlement and the French one under the castle. The open ground between them was built on as the town grew, and became the Old Market Square.[^two] Edward I's charter, approved on 12 February 1284, gave the town its first mayor,[^mayor] with two bailiffs who kept the customs of each borough.[^bho]

bho.title: Thoroton's Nottinghamshire: Nottingham under the government of mayors (British History Online)

groups.title: Charters, markets and fairs, 11th–14th centuries
groups.intro: After the Norman Conquest the right to hold a market was the king's to grant. A charter let the lord take tolls, and no new market could be set up within about a day's travel of an old one.[^charter]

groups.title: Cross and Exchange, 1529–1726
groups.intro: In 1449 the town became a county corporate, governing itself.[^1449]

groups.title: The cheese riot, 1766
groups.intro: Food riots were a familiar part of 18th-century life. In 1766 poor harvests had pushed up the price of grain, and when it began to be shipped abroad that August, riots broke out across England.[^food]

groups.title: From market to shop, 1849–1972
groups.intro: Shops of one name in many towns, the chains, began in the railway age: W. H. Smith opened its first station bookstalls in 1848.[^chain]

layers.title: The Victorian town
layers.intro: In the 19th century Nottingham broke out of its old bounds. In 1877 the borough took in the parishes of Basford, Bulwell, Radford, Sneinton and others round it.[^1877]

fields.title: Expansion (University of Nottingham Manuscripts and Special Collections)

groups.title: A town hemmed in, 1790s–1840s
items: The body snatchers of Barker Gate, 1827
groups.intro: Pressure to enclose the common fields round the town for building began in 1787, but the burgesses who had rights in them, and the owners of town sites, who gained as land grew dearer, held it off until 1845. Building could spread only to a few places, such as Radford, Hyson Green, Sneinton and Carrington, and the framework knitters stayed in the most crowded parts of the town.[^fields]

groups.title: The fields enclosed, 1845–1856
groups.intro: The Inclosure Act of 1845 opened the fields to building, and made room too for a chain of green spaces, among them the Arboretum and the Forest.[^green]

groups.title: Building the lace town, 1865–1898
groups.intro: From 1870 a school board was set up wherever school places fell short, to give children of 5 to 12 an elementary education, though it was not yet free or compulsory.[^1870]

groups.title: A city, 1889–1900
groups.intro: In 1889 Nottingham became a county borough, under the Local Government Act of 1888.[^cb]

layers.title: Crossing the Trent
layers.intro: The Trent is the third-longest river in the United Kingdom, and it once marked the boundary between the north of England and the south.[^trent] Nottingham grew where it could be crossed.

1947.title: Winter of 1946–47 in the United Kingdom

groups.title: Fords, c. 1000 BC–AD 400
groups.intro: Long before any bridge, people crossed where the river ran shallow. The Trent is known for sudden floods after storms and spring snowmelt, and its flood records go back some 900 years.[^floods]

groups.title: A bridge against the Danes, 868–924
groups.intro: Edward the Elder of Wessex ended Danish rule in Nottingham with an assault in the summer of 918.[^five]

groups.title: The medieval bridge, 1156–1683
groups.intro: Medieval bridges often had a chapel on or beside them, where a priest said mass for travellers and for the bridge's benefactors. At the Reformation the Acts of 1545 and 1547 that abolished chantries closed them.[^chapel]

groups.title: From ferries to bridges, 17th century–1906
groups.intro: From 1848 towns could set up boards of health, to look after their sewers, streets and water; the first were a response to cholera.[^health] It was the age of the borough engineer.

groups.title: The river tamed, 1898–1971
groups.intro: In March 1947 snow that had lain all winter thawed fast over frozen ground and ran straight into the rivers; more than 100,000 properties across the country were flooded.[^1947]

layers.title: Science and health
layers.intro: A library and a hospital paid for by subscribers, a miller who taught himself mathematics, engineers who brought clean water, women who fought their way into medicine, and two discoveries that went round the world.

orb.title: Rules of St John's Hospital, Nottingham, 1241 (Florilegium Urbanum, ORB)

groups.title: Almshouses and hospitals, 1241–1392
groups.intro: By 1241 Nottingham's Hospital of St John the Baptist had a rule of life for its brothers and sisters, laid down by Walter de Grey, Archbishop of York;[^orb] it stood at the corner of today's Parliament Street and Glasshouse Street.[^nhh]

groups.title: Learning and healing, 1752–1821
groups.intro: Hospitals of this time were voluntary: they were paid for by subscriptions, gifts and fundraising. By the middle of the 18th century there were six in London.[^vol]

groups.title: Self-taught science, 1793–1880s
groups.intro: From 1821 mechanics' institutes taught working men science and technical subjects, with libraries and apparatus for experiments; by the middle of the century there were over 700 in Britain and abroad.[^mech]

groups.title: Clean water, 1831–1884
groups.intro: Cholera reached Britain in October 1831. The epidemic led in time to the Public Health Act of 1848.[^cholera]

groups.title: Hospitals and asylums, 1857–1880
groups.intro: The Lunacy Act of 1845 made the mentally ill patients, many of whom had been held in gaol as prisoners, and the County Asylums Act of the same year built up a public network of asylums.[^lunacy]

groups.title: A university college, 1877–1928
groups.intro: The university began as an adult school founded in 1798 and lectures given from 1873 by the University of Cambridge in other towns; University College Nottingham was founded in 1881.[^univ]

groups.title: Women in medicine, 1899–1930s
groups.intro: From 11 August 1876 the Medical Act let every British medical authority license qualified applicants, women as well as men.[^1876]

groups.title: Discoveries, 1944–2018
items: A brain scanner you can wear, 2018
groups.intro: Alexander Fleming found penicillin in 1928; Howard Florey and Ernst Chain's team at Oxford made it into a medicine, and the three shared the Nobel Prize in 1945. During the war it became an important part of the Allied effort, saving thousands of lives.[^pen]

layers.title: Soldiers and wars
layers.intro: Nottingham sent soldiers and sailors to wars across the centuries and raised its own county regiment. The two World Wars also reached the city itself, through the munitions factories and depots, the losses at Chilwell and the bombing of 1941.

groups.title: A French marshal on parole, 1705–1711
groups.intro: The War of the Spanish Succession set Britain and its allies against France. At Blenheim on 13 August 1704 the Duke of Marlborough and Eugene of Savoy destroyed a French and Bavarian army; more than 14,000 French soldiers were taken prisoner, among them their commander.[^blen]

groups.title: At sea, 1710–1822
groups.intro: Admiral Sir John Borlase Warren, born at Stapleford, sat as MP for Nottingham from 1797 while still at sea. In October 1798 his squadron, off Donegal, did much to defeat a French fleet sent to invade Ireland. He died in 1822, and has a monument in St Mary's Church, Attenborough.[^warren]

groups.title: The county regiments, 1779–1908
groups.intro: From 1782 regiments of foot were given county names, and Nottinghamshire had two: the 45th, and the 59th, raised in 1755, which became the 2nd Nottinghamshire. The 59th fought in China in the Second Opium War and in Afghanistan in 1878–1880. Under the Childers reforms of 1881 it joined the East Lancashire Regiment.[^59th]

groups.title: War work, 1914–1918
groups.intro: In 1915 a shortage of artillery shells at the front became a political crisis, and Lloyd George was made Minister of Munitions, at the head of a new government department.[^shells] New factories were built to fill shells, Chilwell's among them.

groups.title: Remembering, 1921–1927
groups.intro: After the war thousands of memorials went up across Britain and its empire. The national one, the Cenotaph in Whitehall, was unveiled by George V on 11 November 1920, and many towns modelled theirs on it.[^cenotaph]

groups.title: Getting ready, 1939–1942
groups.intro: Just before the Second World War the RAF built a system of air defence: radar reports went to a filter room, which sifted them into single plots before fighters were sent up. Its fighters were divided into groups, and 12 Group, covering the Midlands, was based at Hucknall and later at Watnall.[^dowding]

groups.title: Bombs and losses, 1941–1943
groups.intro: The Blitz, the German bombing of British cities, ran from 7 September 1940 to 16 May 1941; more than 40,000 civilians were killed by bombing during the war.[^blitz] Nottingham's worst night came in its last fortnight.

layers.title: Statues and memorials
layers.intro: Statues and memorials show who a town chose to honour, and when. Nottingham's range from a Chartist leader and Victorian MPs to the city's war dead and, in the 20th and 21st centuries, figures of legend and football, and at last the women of its past.

njm.title: UK-first bronze sculpture makes history in Nottingham's Broad Marsh Green Heart (National Justice Museum)

groups.title: Victorian heroes, 1859–1905
groups.intro: Nottingham's first public park, the Arboretum, opened on 11 May 1852 on land set aside under the town's Inclosure Act of 1845.[^arb] It became the town's first home for statues: a Chartist MP and the memorial of a county regiment.

groups.title: Between the wars, 1921–1929
groups.intro: After the First World War thousands of memorials went up across Britain and its empire, many of them modelled on the Cenotaph in Whitehall, unveiled on 11 November 1920.[^cenotaph] In Nottingham the war dead came first; then a new Council House gave the Market Square its stone lions.

groups.title: Legend and football, 1952–2008
groups.intro: After the Second World War the city stopped raising statues to its MPs and soldiers, and turned to the figures it was known for around the world: a legendary outlaw and a football manager.

groups.title: Honouring women, 2019–2026
groups.intro: Fewer than one in twenty of Britain's sculptures show a woman who was not royal.[^njm]

layers.title: Art Nouveau
layers.intro: Art Nouveau, the style of curving lines and plant forms that was at its height around 1900, never shaped Nottingham's large buildings, which stayed Gothic or Baroque. It arrived in the details instead: in shopfronts and the tiles of a shop's side wall, in a station's iron gates, and in the porches of ordinary terraced houses.

groups.title: Shops and a station, 1896–1904
groups.intro: Art Nouveau was most popular between 1890 and 1910, and drew on the curves of plants and flowers. In Britain it was also called the Modern Style, and London's Liberty store did much to spread it through its floral fabrics.[^an]

groups.title: Lace money in Long Eaton, 1901–1906
groups.intro: The railways brought Long Eaton its growth, and lace mills went up, Harrington Mill of 1885 among them. By 1907 the town had almost 1,400 lace machines and over 4,000 people, a quarter of its population, worked in lace.[^le]

groups.title: On the doorstep, 1900–1914
groups.intro: Sneinton's population rose from 17,439 in 1891 to its peak of 23,093 in 1901. Land was sold to developers, and the houses they built on the slopes of Sneinton Dale were of a higher standard than the streets before them.[^sn]

layers.title: Lost Nottingham
layers.intro: Much of historic Nottingham has gone. Some buildings were cleared for road schemes and shopping centres in the 20th century; others were destroyed in riots or simply outlived their purpose. These stories record what stood on sites that look very different today.

groups.title: Lost villages, 1276–1779
groups.intro: England has more than 3,000 deserted medieval villages. Many were once thought to have emptied when the Black Death killed their people, but the population was already falling by the early 14th century, and most villages seem to have been abandoned in the 15th; later, enclosure turned fields into sheep pasture and emptied hundreds more.[^dmv]

groups.title: The monks driven out, 1538
groups.intro: Between 1536 and 1541 Henry VIII dissolved the monasteries, priories, convents and friaries of England, Wales and Ireland, seized their wealth and sold their property. Thomas Cromwell ran the work, and in 1536 the Pilgrimage of Grace rose against it in Yorkshire and Lincolnshire.[^diss]

groups.title: Riot and railway, 1829–1904
groups.intro: Riots burned the castle and a mill in 1831. Later in the century the railways took more: Victoria station alone, opened in 1900, needed a 13-acre site and the demolition of some 1,300 houses and 24 pubs.[^vic]

groups.title: Making way, 1926–1960
groups.intro: Between the wars and after the Second World War, old buildings gave way to a new Council House, new roads and new parks, and a village station lost its passengers.

groups.title: The great clearances, 1965–1975
groups.intro: In these years the city centre gained two shopping centres. The Victoria Centre was built from 1967 to 1972 on the site of Victoria station, keeping only its clock tower and hotel, and its 26 floors of flats are still the city's tallest building.[^vc] The Broad Marsh centre followed in 1975.

groups.title: Gone in our time, 2020–2022
groups.intro: Demolition of the Broad Marsh centre began in October 2019. The pandemic stopped the work in March 2020, and its owner, Intu, collapsed that June; in August the council announced it would demolish the rest, at a cost of £8 million.[^bm]

layers.title: Great houses
layers.intro: The countryside around Nottingham was dominated for centuries by landed families: the Cliftons, Pierreponts, Willoughbys and others. Their houses and estates shaped the villages around them, and many were sold, divided or put to new uses in the 20th century.

lost.title: Destruction of country houses in 20th-century Britain

groups.title: Medieval lords, 1257–c. 1500
groups.intro: After 1066 all land in England belonged to the king, who granted its use in return for service. The manor was the basic unit of landholding: its lord had a manor house and demesne land for his own use, and the Domesday Book of 1086 recorded the manors one by one.[^manor]

groups.title: Tudor and Stuart houses, 1523–1677
groups.intro: Between about 1570 and 1620 courtiers and the very rich built "prodigy houses", large and showy, many of them to receive Elizabeth I and her court on their progresses around the country. Wollaton is one of them.[^prodigy]

groups.title: Georgian country houses, 1700s–1790s
groups.intro: Country house building reached its height from the late 17th to the mid-18th century. A house was often designed by one eminent architect in the most fashionable style of the day, and some were built to dominate the land around them.[^country]

groups.title: Victorian estates, 1843–1874
groups.intro: After the Industrial Revolution newly rich industrialists and bankers were eager to show their wealth and taste, and by the 1850s their new mansions were built in one of the many revival styles.[^country]

groups.title: Sold, given away or pulled down, 1933–1965
items: Sold, saved and run by its residents
groups.intro: In the 20th century about one in six of England's country houses was pulled down, some 1,200 since 1900. Two world wars took their servants, and taxes and death duties, raised to new heights after 1945, made them too costly to keep; by 1955 one was being demolished every five days.[^lost]

layers.title: Faith
layers.intro: Nottingham's churches and chapels record a long religious history: the medieval parishes, a priory dissolved at the Reformation, and the growth of Nonconformity and Methodism in the industrial town. William Booth, who founded the Salvation Army, was born here.

groups.title: Before the churches, Roman times–c. 1000
groups.intro: Christianity came to the Anglo-Saxons with the Gregorian mission, which landed in Kent in 597. Mercia, the kingdom that took in Nottingham, turned to it after its pagan king Penda died in 655.[^convert]

groups.title: Domesday and the Norman churches, 1086–1200
groups.intro: After the Conquest of 1066 the Normans brought the Romanesque style, with its round arches, to England. They rebuilt every English cathedral and almost every monastic church, and built hundreds of new parish churches.[^norman]

groups.title: The medieval parishes, 1200s–1400s
groups.intro: English Gothic is read in three styles: Early English, from the late 12th to the late 13th century; Decorated, from the mid-13th to the late 14th; and Perpendicular, from the mid-14th century on.[^gothic]

groups.title: The Reformation, 1535–1539
groups.intro: When the Pope refused to end Henry VIII's marriage to Catherine of Aragon, Parliament abolished the Pope's authority in England and made the king supreme head of the Church of England. The break with Rome gave the Crown control of the Church, and then of its monasteries.[^reform]

groups.title: War and rebuilding, 1643–1779
groups.intro: After the Civil War and the Restoration, the Act of Uniformity of 1662 required every minister to be ordained by a bishop and to follow the Book of Common Prayer. Over 2,000 clergymen refused and were expelled from their churches: the Great Ejection.[^unif]

groups.title: Chapels and Methodism, 1690–1839
groups.intro: The Toleration Act received royal assent on 24 May 1689. It let Protestant dissenters, such as Baptists, Congregationalists and Presbyterians, worship in their own meeting houses, once these were registered and their preachers licensed. It did not apply to Roman Catholics.[^toler]

groups.title: Churches for new districts, 1812–1903
groups.intro: Parliament's Church Building Act of 1818 gave £1 million for new churches, mainly in growing industrial towns where people had outrun the churches, and a second grant of £500,000 followed in 1824.[^cba]

groups.title: Missions and the Salvation Army, 1829–1909
groups.intro: On one Sunday in 1851 the census counted everyone at worship across England and Wales: 10,896,066 attendances, out of a population of 17,927,609. Fewer than half were at the Church of England, and the count was never repeated.[^census]

layers.title: Freemasons
layers.intro: Freemasons have met in Nottingham since the 1750s: first in the town's inns, later in a hall of their own on Goldsmith Street, which is still the home of the county's lodges.

groups.title: Lodges in the inns, 1755–1844
groups.intro: The first Grand Lodge was formed in London in 1717. In 1751 six lodges set up a rival Grand Lodge, the Antients, and the two were not united until 1813, as the United Grand Lodge of England.[^antients]

groups.title: Dukes and foundation stones, 1863–1898
groups.intro: Nottinghamshire's Freemasons were led by dukes. The 6th Duke of Newcastle was installed as Provincial Grand Master at the Mechanics' Hall in Nottingham in January 1866.[^newcastle] In 1863 there were only four lodges in the town: in order of seniority, the Newstead, the Royal Sussex, the Commercial and the Pelham.[^portland]

groups.title: A hall of their own, 1880–1930
groups.intro: Freemasonry grew fast around the First World War: between 1910 and 1928 the number of Freemasons in the world doubled, to about 4,400,000.[^cl]

layers.title: Women's lives
layers.intro: Women's lives in Nottingham are less recorded than men's, but they appear throughout its history: as writers, businesswomen, teachers, doctors, nurses and librarians, and as campaigners for the vote.

groups.title: Votes for women
groups.intro: Nottingham had an active women's suffrage movement from the 1890s. Some women worked for change through peaceful campaigning; others, as suffragettes, took direct action and were imprisoned.

groups.title: Work and care
groups.intro: From Lucy Hutchinson in the 17th century to the doctors, nurses and engineers of the 20th, women in Nottingham wrote, ran businesses and schools, cared for the sick and wounded and led professional institutions, often as the first women to do so.

layers.title: Writers and artists
layers.intro: Nottinghamshire has produced or attracted a number of notable writers and artists. Their work often draws on the life of the area, from the Byrons and the Romantic poets to the mining communities of D. H. Lawrence and the working-class Nottingham of Alan Sillitoe.

groups.title: Writers
groups.intro: Writers connected with Nottingham include Lucy Hutchinson in the 17th century, Byron and Henry Kirke White in the Romantic period, and in the 20th century D. H. Lawrence, born in Eastwood, and Alan Sillitoe, whose novel Saturday Night and Sunday Morning is set in the city.

groups.title: Artists
groups.intro: Painters and photographers have also come from the area, among them Richard Parkes Bonington, born in Arnold; today Nottingham Contemporary shows art in the city.

layers.title: Sport
layers.intro: Nottingham has a long sporting history. Trent Bridge became one of England's main cricket grounds, the city is home to two of the oldest football clubs in the world, and its sportsmen and women have included prize-fighters, rowers and ice dancers.

groups.title: Cricket
groups.intro: Cricket was played behind the Trent Bridge Inn from 1838, and the ground became the home of Nottinghamshire and a Test venue from 1899. Nottinghamshire players were among the leading cricketers of their day, and two of its fast bowlers were central to the Bodyline series of 1932–33.

groups.title: Football
groups.intro: Notts County, founded in 1862, and Nottingham Forest, founded in 1865, are among the oldest professional clubs in the world. Their grounds face each other across the Trent. Forest won the FA Cup in 1898 and, under Brian Clough, the European Cup in 1979 and 1980.

groups.title: Other sports
groups.intro: Nottingham's sporting history also includes the bare-knuckle boxer William "Bendigo" Thompson, a Derby winner, the international rowing course at Holme Pierrepont and the ice dancers Jayne Torvill and Christopher Dean.
